item.title: Russia stonewalls U.S. as Trump administration weighs risks from mysterious lab death
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks during a press conference at the House of Collections in Reykjavik, Iceland, on October 6, 2026. - Mark Schiefelbein/Pool/AFP/Getty Images The Trump administration is struggling to get clear answers about the death of a Russian laboratory worker at an institute dedicated to studying the plague and has formally escalated its request for information from the country, amid days of stonewalling from Russian officials about the mysterious circumstances surrounding the episode. The death of the technician at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia immediately raised alarms throughout the administration, prompting a race to compile intel and plot for a potential public health response, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter. But Russia’s reluctance to share information about the incident has complicated those efforts, leaving officials uncertain what broader risks it could pose — and how exactly to defend the US against them. The US escalated its request for information, issuing a formal diplomatic communication, called a démarche, a source familiar told CNN late Tuesday. “We have officially requested additional information from the Russian government,” a State Department spokesperson said. “We are also in official communication with other countries around the world to share information.” “It’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said earlier Tuesday . “Maybe it’s bigger than we thought. We don’t know, but I think it would be reckless at this moment, given the limited information we still have, to speculate.” US officials were in touch with the Russian government as early as last Friday, a State Department official said, including contact between the department’s health experts and the Russian Foreign Ministry. And that outreach has continued, an administration official said, as Rubio expressed hope Tuesday that the limited information sharing “will change in the next few hours and days.” President Donald Trump told reporters outside the White House Tuesday afternoon that he had “call scheduled” to speak with Russian leader Vladimir Putin about the issue “very soon.” He added US agencies would have more information to report “probably tomorrow.” But the US has gotten limited cooperation so far. What little information has come out of Russia has faced deep skepticism, with officials unconvinced that the Kremlin is being fully forthcoming, according to people familiar with the situation. Still, until the administration knows more through intelligence collection and diplomatic outreach, officials are not taking steps such as putting travel restrictions into place to prevent any potential spread, according to a US official. The US already advises against travel to Russia due to various factors, including the possibility of wrongful detention and the war with Ukraine. Among the critical questions still outstanding: whether the 28-year-old lab worker who died last week contracted pneumonic plague — a severe but treatable infection — or another, unknown infectious disease. Staff at the Anti-Plague Institute study a range of other dangerous diseases, including cholera, anthrax and brucellosis, according to the institute’s website . US officials have also sought details on whether the disease was modified in any way, a process called gain of function that could dramatically alter the way the US and other countries might respond. Rubio and other Trump officials have publicly downplayed the immediate threat to Americans, emphasizing that the administration is closely monitoring the situation and that pneumonic plague is treatable with antibiotics. But behind the scenes, there is deep unease within the administration over the continued lack of insight, the people familiar with the situation said. Compounding those concerns is the Russian government’s outsized response, including quarantining the hospital where the lab worker was treated, according to the mayor of the Shelekhovsky district. Nearly 200 people are under observation , a regional news outlet reported. The entrance to the grounds of the anti-plague institute in the city of Irkutsk, Russia, on October 6, 2026. - AFP/Getty Images “We don’t know a lot right now about what actually happened,” said one US official. “But one thing most of us feel certain about: The Russians are going to act like the Chinese did with Covid. They won’t be forthcoming.” Still, Trump on Monday characterized the situation as a “big problem” for Russia, suggesting that the US might need to provide some unspecified level of aid. In a statement, a State Department spokesperson said that several federal agencies were “closely monitoring the fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague,” but that many of the details surrounding it remained unconfirmed. They reiterated that Americans have long been advised not to travel to Russia for any reason. “We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly,” the spokesperson said. In the days since the lab worker’s death, the National Security Council and State Department officials have led the administration’s push to gather information, piece together what happened and evaluate the potential risks, officials and others familiar with the situation said. Federal health agencies, including the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response, have also been involved in the cross-government effort. A source familiar with the outreach said Trump officials have also backchanneled with the World Health Organization — the international health body that Trump pulled funding from soon after taking office, but that the government has continued to communicate with in emergency situations. WHO said Monday that it was in contact with Russian authorities to verify details about the lab worker’s death, though it has so far also received little information. “If they’re not transparent, if they’re not open to independent accountability, how is it possible to trust the Kremlin is telling us the full and accurate information?” said Lawrence Gostin, a global health law professor at Georgetown University who has worked closely with WHO. “Clearly, on its face, the lab was conducting extremely high-risk research and using shoddy biosafety measures.” The Anti-Plague Institute’s relatively remote location in eastern Russia, combined with the pneumonic plague’s limited ability to quickly spread, has given health experts some comfort that any immediate threat can be contained. Pneumonic plague is a bacterial infection , unlike the highly transmissible coronavirus strain that sparked the 2020 pandemic. And while the plague is fatal if untreated, there are now effective and widely available antibiotics to treat it. While there is little indication that the incident will touch off another global health crisis, officials and outside experts said it has nevertheless reinforced how difficult it can be to monitor and prepare for potential biological threats. The Health and Human Services Department may have the medical stockpile necessary to combat conventional pneumonic plague, those officials and experts said. But there’s little certainty whether it could do the same against a modified version — or how long it would take to develop a treatment if needed. Jennifer Nuzzo, an epidemiology professor and director of the Pandemic Center at Brown University School of Public Health, said the episode also comes as health response capabilities both in the US and globally have been diminished by funding cuts and the strain of responding to other crises. WHO has proposed slashing its budget following a $600 million shortfall triggered by the US’ exit. America’s ability to handle a new public health response, meanwhile, “is severely diminished” amid its efforts to combat measles outbreaks, she said. “We are talking about a very depleted system. God forbid you layer another pathogen onto the already laborious and difficult work of going after measles,” said Nuzzo. “That would be a nightmare.” This story has been updated with additional details. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/06/politics/russia-plague-death-trump

item.title: Will Trump's executive order on dyed diesel lower prices? Experts explain.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump has issued an executive order that makes a specific kind of tax-exempt diesel fuel reserved for farm and construction equipment available to a broad set of road vehicles in an effort to reduce overall diesel costs . The type of diesel, known as dyed diesel, is exempt from a 24.4-cent per gallon federal tax, making it a lower-priced option than regular diesel. Some states expanded access to dyed diesel in a similar fashion over recent weeks, providing relief from state diesel taxes. Dyed diesel is nearly identical to regular diesel, besides a small amount of dye used by law enforcement officers and inspectors to ensure only permitted vehicle owners avail themselves of the fuel. Should you use your 401(k) to pay off credit card debt? The executive order on Monday came weeks ahead of the midterm elections, targeting costs associated with a fuel vital to the supply chain for everything from groceries to clothing to electronics. The White House called on federal agencies to defer payment of federal road taxes over the remainder of 2026, and seek out ways to relieve payment of the deferred taxes. "Farmers and truckers are essential to the American way of life. Restricted global diesel supply has led to rising prices, and these key industries have been particularly hard hit," the White House said in its executive order. "While my Administration has already undertaken historic efforts to ensure fuel affordability for our citizens, it is clear that further temporary relief is necessary," the White House added. In theory, a meaningful reduction in diesel prices could lower expenses for farmers and truckers, while easing the cost burden for shoppers crunched by a rise of inflation. A host of factors will complicate the effectiveness of the order, however, some analysts told ABC News. Dyed diesel is sold at a limited set of locations designed primarily for industry operators, constraining access to the fuel. Expansion of vehicles eligible for dyed diesel, meanwhile, could prompt a surge in demand for the fuel, exceeding available supply and putting upward pressure on prices at the pump, some analysts said. "On paper and in the press, it sounds like it might be significant, especially ahead of the midterms. However, like many things, the paper doesn’t always match the intended reality," Patrick De Haan, a petroleum analyst at GasBuddy, said in a post on Substack . Charlie Riedel/AP Photo - PHOTO: Trump All in all, analysts who spoke to ABC News downplayed the potential impact of Trump's decree, saying savings would be modest for farmers, who already enjoy access to dyed diesel for their energy-intensive agricultural equipment. The move could shed nearly 25 cents per gallon from the cost of diesel for vehicle owners newly allowed to access the tax-exempt fuel, but those savings make up a small share of the price increase for diesel set off by the Iran war, analysts said. The average price of a gallon of diesel stands at $6.31, marking an increase of $2.63, or about 70%, from a year earlier, AAA data shows. A truck with a 150-gallon tank, for example, runs its owner about $948 for a fill-up at current diesel prices. A deduction of 24.4 cents per gallon would remove $36 from that bill. "This is a way to try to use executive power to try to provide short-term relief," said Timothy Fitzgerald, a University of Tennessee professor of business economics who studies the petroleum industry. "But you’ve seen a very large increase in retail prices. The tax relief will help but it won’t offset the underlying difference in prices." Meanwhile, the savings will likely be muted or nonexistent for products on store shelves, analysts added, since diesel prices make up a fraction of the costs that feed into the price of any given product. Every dollar spent on food, for instance, usually includes three or four cents that stem from transportation costs, Omair Sharif, founder of Inflation Insights, previously told ABC News. David Ortega, a food economist at Michigan State University, said he expects any potential price relief on grocery store shelves to be "negligible." "If you look at how the price of fuel factors into overall food costs, we’re talking about a single-digit [percentage] share of overall food costs. This is not something that will really be driving prices down meaningfully," Ortega added. Tom Seng, a professor of energy finance at Texas Christian University, echoed the view. "I don’t think this will be significant enough that we’ll see food prices in general come down," Seng told ABC News. Trump says his super PAC will now pay for controversial taxpayer-funded promotional ads To be sure, the price savings for eligible diesel buyers could prove more significant in states that offered up an exemption from state-level taxes, compounding the benefit of the federal tax exemption. A handful of states have granted their own waiver for dyed diesel, including important midterm states like Nebraska, North Carolina and Texas, De Haan said. Georgia and Ohio recently suspended their diesel taxes, offering their own version of relief. The state-by-state policy differences could pose a challenge for interstate truckers, however, deterring some vehicle owners who fear local law enforcement, De Haan said. Various impediments will limit the effect of the executive order, Ortega said. "It’s not really going to make a whole lot of difference," he added. item.title: Christa Pike survived her execution. A 1947 case could shape what comes next.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
With the astonishing news that Christa Pike is conscious, talking and making a "medically unprecedented" recovery following her botched execution , Tennessee is now facing a critical question: Will the state try to kill her again? "Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care," her attorneys said in a statement on Oct. 6. "Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery." So far, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has not responded to repeated calls from Pike's attorneys and death penalty observers to commute her sentence to life in prison. That leaves open the possibility that Pike will face a second execution, even after her attorneys said the first attempt on Sept. 30 amounted to unconstitutionally cruel and unusual punishment. "We’re in uncharted territory," said Robin Maher, executive director of the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center, which does not take a stance on the death penalty. "The U.S. Supreme Court has not decided whether a second execution attempt would violate the constitution since 1947," Maher told USA TODAY. “These are questions that have never needed to be asked before and no one knows the answers.” As Pike continues to recover in a Tennessee hospital, USA TODAY is looking at the issues that state officials will need to weigh when deciding whether Pike will live or die. When did the Supreme Court last address a second execution? The last time the Supreme Court addressed whether an inmate who survived an execution would face another one was nearly 80 years ago in 1947. The case involved Willie Francis, a 17-year-old Black teen convicted of murder by an all-white jury for a crime committed when he was 16. His first execution inside the local parish jail in St. Martinville, Louisiana, was halted when the portable electric chair known as "Gruesome Gertie" failed to deliver enough current. It was widely reported that the electrical mechanism malfunctioned due to improper setup by a drunken prison guard. Witnesses said Francis screamed "Take it off! Take it off! Let me breathe!" from behind his leather hood. The execution was aborted, and an appeal was filed to the Supreme Court. Francis spent the next year back on death row awaiting a decision from the Supreme Court about whether a second electrocution would be unconstitutional cruel and unusual punishment, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. The court justices ruled that the state could put Francis back in the electric chair, writing that "accidents happen for which no man is to blame." "Even the fact that (Francis) has already been subjected to a current of electricity does not make his subsequent execution any more cruel in the constitutional sense than any other execution," the Supreme Court concluded. "The cruelty against which the Constitution protects a convicted man is cruelty inherent in the method of punishment, not the necessary suffering involved in any method employed to extinguish life humanely." Francis was successfully executed in the electric chair on May 9, 1947. He told reporter Elliott Chaze a few days before the execution that he was going to meet the Lord with his "Sunday pants and Sunday heart." Experts: Pike's case differs from 1947 case There's a huge difference between what happened to Francis in 1947 and what happened to Pike last week, said Columbia Law School's Bernard Harcourt , who is writing a book about a botched lethal injection in Alabama involving an inmate he represented. “What’s interesting about that case is that the Supreme Court said it was an accident and, ‘You get to do it again,’” Harcourt told USA TODAY. “Christa Pike wasn’t an accident. They knew. They had information from her lawyers, who told them, ‘You’re going to have a hard time getting to her veins .’” Nearly 10 months before the Pike's botched execution, Pike's attorneys warned Tennessee that personnel would have trouble with Pike's unusually small veins and would struggle to deliver a fatal dose of pentobarbital. They repeated those warnings up until her execution. Because of that, Harcourt said, if Tennessee seeks to try to execute Pike again, it would "arguably violate double jeopardy." Maher of the Death Penalty Information Center agreed that a second attempt would "likely be unconstitutional." "Of all the unknowns we have at the moment, the only thing I’m certain of is that she should not be subject to a second one," Maher said. "She has already endured a torturous experience in that execution chamber." Chaos in the death chamber: Timeline of Christa Pike's botched execution Tennessee governor hasn't ruled out 2nd execution for previous botch In May, Tennessee botched another execution. Tony Carruthers survived after executioners failed to establish a second IV line required under the state's execution protocol. The doctor carrying out the lethal injection also unsuccessfully tried to place a central line. After Carruthers spent more than an hour strapped down waiting to die, the state abandoned the execution. Lee granted Carruthers a rare one-year reprieve, leaving open the option to try to execute him again. In a lawsuit filed in July , his family said that they believe Carruthers suffered a brain stroke and that the entire right side of his body was left paralyzed. His attorneys argue that he's suffered enough and that the governor should commute his sentence. He has not. As for Pike's botched execution, Lee ordered an investigation into what went wrong, called off the state's only remaining lethal injection this year and announced the upcoming resignation of Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada . Lee has not granted Pike a reprieve similar to Carruthers' and has not indicated what the future holds for her. He hasn't spoken publicly about the matter since Oct. 1, the day after the botched execution. Lee called the failure a deeply disturbing "tragedy" that should never have happened. He also reiterated his commitment to the death penalty. "My responsibility is to uphold the sentences that Tennessee juries have handed down, even when it's difficult, and that is exactly what we intend to do in the days ahead," Lee said. "The people of Tennessee have determined that the death penalty is the appropriate penalty for the most heinous crimes in the state. The people of Tennessee make that decision, and my job is to make sure then that those sentences are carried out." A recap of the case Tennessee was supposed to execute Pike, 50, by lethal injection on Sept. 30 for the brutal and prolonged 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. The execution failed after Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital injections and was taken to a Nashville-area hospital. A timeline of the chaos in the death chamber compiled by USA TODAY shows that the state tried to kill Pike for over an hour before rushing to save her. Her attorneys say they believe that Pike's IV lines were improperly placed or that Pike's veins had blown, causing some or all of the pentobarbital to enter her arm rather than her bloodstream. The state has not said why Pike's execution failed. Pike was 18 when she and her 17-year-old boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, lured Slemmer into the woods in Knoxville on Jan. 12, 1995. Prosecutors said Pike and Shipp tortured and killed Slemmer, who was her romantic rival. Pike cut Slemmer's throat and crushed her skull with a rock, later showing off a piece of the skull. Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, witnessed Pike's failed execution. Martinez previously told People Magazine that Pike had never apologized for her daughter's death and that she wanted to finally see justice. Contributing: Kelly Puente , Nashville Tennessean Amanda Lee Myers is a senior crime and courts reporter who covers the death penalty, cold cases and breaking news for USA TODAY. Follow her on X at @amandaleeusat . This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: 'Uncharted territory': Will Tennessee try to kill Christa Pike again? This article originally appeared on USA TODAY at https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2026/10/06/tennessee-execution-christa-pike-second-attempt-botch/92127144007/

item.title: Trump allies push to sideline AI safety advocates as fight over oversight grows
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
BERKELEY, Calif. - After artificial intelligence safety advocates captured Washington’s attention with dire warnings about the technology’s power, the Trump administration and its allies embraced some of their suggestions, while moving to sideline the advocates themselves. Battle lines have been drawn in recent days over part of an accord signed by President Donald Trump and AI chief executives last week: Who should audit AI companies’ systems to ensure their technology behaves as intended. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Leading AI companies - including OpenAI and Anthropic - have for years worked with a cluster of nonprofits concentrated in the Bay Area’s AI safety community, which grew out of the effective altruism movement. But Trump’s tech-world allies say the work of auditing AI should be taken on by America’s largest consulting firms. “In my view they should be professional auditors, not these NGOs,” investor and former top White House AI adviser David Sacks said on his All-In podcast last week. He said in a post on X last month that the AI safety nonprofit METR, which has worked with Anthropic, was too close to the company to be called independent. Soon after, Anthropic said it would partner with consulting giant Accenture to build a team of outside evaluators. At a conference here over the weekend, members of AI safety organizations grappled with the impact of what some see as a coordinated campaign to delegitimize their work and paint their community as cultish and unserious. The event took place at a former hotel popular with AI safety acolytes that also recently hosted a conference on AI consciousness and a sex workshop called “Slutcon.” Trump officials and allies have sniped at the movement for months but the attacks intensified after public anxiety over AI risks forced the White House to respond. Sacks last month shared on X a New York Post front page that called employees of METR, which helped OpenAI investigate its rogue AI agents, “THE WOKE WIZARDS OF AI.” (The Washington Post has a content partnership with OpenAI.) Trump on Sunday named several figures who have rejected calls from advocates for an AI industry-wide slowdown to his Super Intelligence Force advisory panel. They include Sacks and Emil Michael, the Pentagon’s chief technology officer, who said last month that calls for action to prevent extreme scenarios of AI causing harm promoted “extinction, death-cult-like philosophies.” “There has absolutely been a rhetorical push within certain corners of the White House and broader Trump administration to get the message out about effective altruism and its potential dangers,” said a Trump administration official, speaking on the condition of anonymity to describe private discussions. A White House official said that it supports organizations that evaluate the security and safety of how AI models are engineered. The official pointed to Trump’s 2025 executive order targeting what the president termed “woke AI.” Anthropic declined to comment. Nathan Leamer, director of the pro-industry nonprofit Build American AI, said he has been briefing congressional staff and other influential conservative figures in Washington about effective altruism, describing it as antithetical to his own Christian values. “A year ago no one in Hill offices knew what effective altruism was,” Leamer said. Build American AI is linked to Leading the Future, a political campaign group funded by the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz and OpenAI President Greg Brockman, a major midterms Republican donor. Brad Carson, co-founder of Americans for Responsible Innovation, which says it is focused on AI policy in the public interest, said that Trump allies are trying discredit anyone pushing for meaningful AI regulation, an idea that now has significant momentum. “In D.C., at least, and maybe in the broader culture, we won that fight. The vibe is with us,” said Carson, who also leads a political advocacy organization funded in part by Anthropic. “People are very concerned. Congress wants to regulate.” But leaders of AI evaluation start-ups that did not grow out of the AI safety movement said some Washington Republicans are distrustful of the label. “It almost felt like a new version of McCarthyism,” said Rayan Krishnan, CEO of the Andreessen Horowitz-backed start-up Vals AI, after a trip to Washington last month to pitch his start-up to the public sector. Judd Rosenblatt, CEO of AE Studio, who described himself as a conservative small business owner, said multiple people in the Trump administration have told his team that they see the need for third parties to assess AI tools, but are wary of effective altruism, he said. Civil society groups that have been auditing AI systems since before the debut of ChatGPT warn there is a risk that an opportunity for oversight of opaque AI giants will be squandered. “Where we find ourselves now is trying to determine who will actually be in the room in making decisions,” said Miranda Bogen, chief technologist at the Center for Democracy & Technology and director of the advocacy group’s AI Governance Lab, one of various groups eager to contribute their expertise in standard-setting. The accord signed by AI chief executives last week, which Trump called “morally binding,” was frequently mentioned onstage and in huddles between sessions at the Berkeley conference last weekend, where attendees endured a heat wave with fans and Popsicles. At a Sunday discussion panel on what the AI auditor ecosystem might look like, one speaker said they are working on building a broad coalition of experts, including people working on bias and discrimination as well as blue-chip firms like Accenture and Deloitte. Panelists also discussed other ways the community could prove its legitimacy. Another suggested two-month boot camps to train a talent pipeline of qualified auditors. Adam Gleave, CEO of FAR.AI, a nonprofit research institute, said in an interview that excluding the AI safety community would shut out people with expertise that are important in the current moment. “When it comes to looking at millions of agent transcripts and trying to piece together what they did and how they were interacting, I don’t think there are many organizations in the world that have that expertise,” Gleave said. “The reality is that anyone you hire with that background is going to have some connection to the industry.” On his podcast, Sacks and his co-hosts, who remain close to the White House, made clear that they preferred instead to have established corporate giants do the work. “You’re going to see EY in short order here announce something,” said investor Chamath Palihapitiya, who earlier in the episode said his start-up 8090 was building the global accounting firm formerly known as Ernst & Young “an entire audit infrastructure for super intelligence,” and that 8090 now plans to “roll it out to everybody.” EY said in a statement that it was working with 8090 to “develop new capabilities that bring greater visibility, traceability and human accountability to consequential AI-enabled decisions and workflows.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/told-world-ai-dangerous-now-092510605.html

item.title: S&P 500 hits record high as Nvidia nears $6 trillion milestone
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange during morning trading last month. (Michael M. Santiago / Getty) The S&P 500 hit a record Tuesday as it rose for a fourth straight day, supported by rising technology stocks, hopes for a positive earnings season and a pause in oil’s recent surge. The broad-based index closed higher by 0.58%, its first record closing high since Aug. 13. The Nasdaq Composite also jumped 0.45%. It also hit a record high for the second time this week. The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq’s gains were overwhelmingly powered by gains in tech companies, such as chipmakers Marvell and Broadcom. Nvidia, the world’s largest public company, also rose and moved closer to becoming the first company to ever reach $6 trillion in market value. Other trillion-dollar tech stocks also rose Tuesday. Microsoft, Amazon, SpaceX, Meta Platforms and Tesla shares all traded in the green. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang delivers the keynote address at the GTC AI Conference in San Jose, Calif., last year. (Josh Edelson / AFP via Getty) Investors are also looking forward to the start of the third quarter’s earnings season, which begins in earnest next week with the country’s biggest banks reporting their results. “Heading into the start of the earnings season, analysts and companies have been more optimistic than normal in their earnings outlooks for the third quarter,” said FactSet senior earnings analyst John Butters. Artificial intelligence stocks are set to be a major contributor. “At the stock level, AI infrastructure stocks are expected to drive more than half of S&P 500 EPS growth in Q3,” analysts at Goldman Sachs said Friday. They forecast that Nvidia and chipmaker Micron would most likely be responsible for a third of the entire S&P 500’s earnings growth this quarter. Oil static Stocks got off to a strong start Tuesday thanks to a drop in oil prices. However, by the end of the trading day, energy prices were about flat. That did little to deter the rally in stocks, though. Brent oil futures ended the day up 0.2%, at $100.58 per barrel, but that came after an earlier drop of as much as 3.3%. U.S. crude oil ended the day up just 1 cent, at $89.44 per barrel. Earlier, it was down more than 2.8%. Oil’s session was muted after Bloomberg News reported that Saudi Arabia’s key cross-country pipeline was operating normally, after “multiple attacks” took the critical pipeline out of commission in early September. Saudi Aramco has not responded to multiple requests for comment. Three-phase spheroids stand behind pipelines at Saudi Aramco's crude oil processing facility in Abqaiq, Saudi Arabia, in 2019. (Dina Khrennikova / Bloomberg via Getty) The pipeline has been used as a Strait of Hormuz workaround, given that shipping traffic there remains at just a fraction of pre-Iran war levels. Still, “the market remains nervous about potential supply disruptions from the region,” ING commodities analysts overnight said. “This nervousness is likely to persist until there are signs of progress in a deal between the US and Iran. In the meantime, the risk of further escalation remains very real.” Bond watch Treasury yields also declined slightly after they hit fresh 24-year highs Monday. The 10-year yield was still at more than 5.27%. The 30-year Treasury was about flat, at 5.6%. While the yields, or the rate, on both of those bonds have been at their highest levels since 2002, some experts think they’re close to topping out. “Several forces suggest rates may peak within the next month,” Apollo’s Torsten Slok said Tuesday. “Approaching midterm elections raise the odds of a Middle East deal that would lower oil prices.” President Donald Trump has said multiple times recently that he believes a deal could be reached with Iran to end the seven-month war “right after” the midterm elections are over . “Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward,” Trump said Sept. 9. Those comments marked a turn after he had said for months that the war would last only a short period. Slok said, “A deal or government action that lowers oil prices would ease the upward pressure on interest rates at a time when yields are already elevated across nearly the entire global bond market.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/business/markets/stocks-records-oil-nvidia-rcna601852

item.title: Trump doesn't commit to repaying $12 million in federal funds spent on controversial ads
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — A day after President Donald Trump said he would start paying for controversial taxpayer-funded ads with a campaign account, there's no sign he plans to refund the millions of federal dollars already spent on them. Nearly $12 million worth of ads have already aired, according to AdImpact, as part of the $20 million the Department of Homeland Security tapped for the contract . But Trump's plan to pay for the ads with MAGA Inc. doesn't mean there's any reimbursement coming, said a White House official who was not authorized to talk publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity. Speaking to reporters Tuesday, Trump said the ads were "really good" and "promotion for the country, done by many presidents before." Asked whether he'd repay the funds already spent, he said, "We'll decide." Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer slammed Trump for not committing to reimbursement and said he believes the president's plan for covering future costs represents illegal coordination with his super PAC. "Trump must return this money to the American people and there must be a full investigation into this gross waste and abuse of taxpayer dollars," Schumer told The Associated Press. The ads, which began airing in late September, glorify Trump and echo his political messaging going into the midterms. One features a clip of Trump talking about the threat of communism and another is a replay of an ad from his last presidential campaign. The fifth ad in the campaign began airing Tuesday, focusing on the Trump administration's capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro . Republicans and Democrats alike have said the ads aren't an appropriate use of U.S. government money. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a Republican from South Dakota, said they shouldn't be paid for with taxpayer dollars. The Trump administration tapped $20 million from the Department of Homeland Security to pay for the campaign-style ads glorifying the president that have drawn widespread criticism . Two top Democratic senators said last week that the money is being drawn from Trump's so-called "One Big Beautiful Bill" and was supposed to go toward U.S. Customs and Border Protection. Republican Sen. Katie Britt of Alabama, who chairs the panel that oversees DHS funding, said Tuesday that she had not yet seen Trump's ads, but she said taxpayer money should be used as intended. "We'll take a look at that," Britt said at the Capitol. "You want to make sure that any use of taxpayer dollars is done judiciously and in accordance with the law." Legal experts said the ads might even violate federal statutes, including a law against congressionally appropriated money being used for "publicity or propaganda" and another limiting the partisan political activities of government employees. The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements similar to what past administrations have done to promote policies. Trump on Monday posted on his Truth Social platform calling the ads "positive promotion for our Great U.S.A." while also promising to pay for them with "money I raised for MAGA Inc." That is Trump's political war chest , which had amassed more than $400 million by the end of July. Trump has begun tapping it to boost Republican candidates across the country in the midterm elections. ___ AP Congressional Correspondent Lisa Mascaro contributed to this report. item.title: Trump administration unveils plan to tie high birth and marriage rates to transit funding
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Communities with high birth and marriage rates could soon gain an advantage in securing federal transit money — a long-sought goal of the Trump administration but one that a top Democratic appropriator calls "bizarre and dystopian." The Federal Transit Administration wants to revamp a multibillion-dollar program that helps state and local authorities fund infrastructure projects such as rail improvements and new bus lanes. Public feedback on the administration's plan, which was rolled out Oct. 1, is being accepted through mid-November. The idea would fulfill a priority of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy to steer grant money to parts of the country with birth and marriage rates higher than the national average, a policy initiative he unveiled shortly after being sworn into office early last year . Under the transit proposal , the FTA would cover up to 10 percentage points more of a project's costs if an area's average birth and marriage rates meet, exceed or are just below nationwide thresholds. "Moving forward, the federal government is focusing on smart, affordable projects with high ridership. If you want federal funding, your project needs to align with where communities and families are actually growing," the Transportation Department said in a statement. But the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee had harsh words for the proposal. "Tying funding for transit projects to marriage rates and how many babies a woman has is the sort of bizarre and dystopian idea you'd expect in a TV show, not actual policy put forth by the U.S. government — yet here we are," Sen. Patty Murray of Washington state said in a statement. She said President Donald Trump "wants to weaponize federal grants to wage his backward culture wars and punish Democrats." Spokespeople for Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.), ranking member of the House Appropriations Committee, didn't respond to a request for comment. A former FTA administrator during the Obama administration also was critical. "It's throwing a bone to these ideologues who want to incentivize child rearing and marriage," said Peter Rogoff, who previously led Sound Transit in the Seattle area and is now a transportation consultant. "But it's ludicrous on its face to try to achieve that goal through an infrastructure program. "Does anyone really believe that there are couples out there saying, 'Hey, sweetheart, you and I should get married and raise a passel of kids because a dozen years from now, maybe they'll build light rail out to our neighborhood?'" he asked. Duffy, who has nine children, has urged young people to tie the knot and " have lots of kids ." He's one of several Cabinet members with big families, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, DHS head Markwayne Mullin and Health and Human Services chief Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The national fertility rate sank to a record low in 2025 — 53.1 births per 1,000 women ages 15 to 44. Trump has said he will be known as the "fertilization president." The FTA grant program hinges on a lengthy approval process that can take years for applicants to navigate, with money becoming available after a binding grant agreement is executed. Before reaching the final step, the FTA determines how much of a project's total cost it will cover. The share of federal funding is capped at 60 percent for new, large transit infrastructure and 80 percent for boosting the capacity of existing systems. For those two types of projects, the administration now wants to calculate the amount it will fund using a formula that, in part, would be based on a transit corridor's average birth and marriage rates. When those rates are at or above national benchmarks, or just below them, the federal share would be increased — rising by up to 10 percentage points. Under Duffy, DOT has launched a "Make Travel Family Friendly Again" campaign, encouraging airports to create play areas and add nursing rooms at terminals. He also has sought to inspire families to travel around the country via his "The Great American Road Trip" video series . The birth and marriage rates proposal has yet to be finalized, and it's unknown when it will be. It also wasn't immediately clear which exact communities would benefit from the idea. The plan is part of a wider effort by the FTA to rewrite its guidance for federal Capital Investment Grants, or CIG. The public can weigh in through Nov. 16. CIG and a related pilot initiative got $1.7 billion from Congress for fiscal 2026 on top of $1.6 billion in additional funding from the 2021 bipartisan infrastructure law. Projects that previously won money from the program include the ongoing construction of the Gateway rail tunnel between New York and New Jersey and a pending extension of Chicago's Red Line train . Paul Skoutelas, CEO and president of the American Public Transportation Association, said in a statement the organization is reviewing the FTA plan. Rogoff, the former FTA administrator, said the framework would "clearly disadvantage" projects in areas with lower birth and marriage rates, adding that federal law doesn't require that this data be relied on when carrying out CIG. "Obviously, the program is about moving people — not about moving married people or moving parents," he said. item.title: Trump looms over Susan Collins and Troy Jackson's first Maine Senate debate
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Susan Collins; Troy Jackson. (Getty) Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson debated for the first time Tuesday in Maine, trading attacks over President Donald Trump, the cost of living and abortion in one of the most closely watched Senate races in the country . Maine is central to Democrats’ path to the Senate majority as they try to capitalize on Trump’s unpopularity. Jackson tried to do just that Tuesday by tying Collins to Trump, name-checking him at least 20 times in one hour of debating on WGME-TV. “It matters who you stand with,” Jackson said in his opening statement. “I don’t owe Donald Trump and the billionaires anything. I don’t fight for billionaires like she does.” Collins, meanwhile, emphasized multiple instances when she opposed the Trump administration. She also sought to localize the race and pitch her seniority — and her perch as chair of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee — as a boost to Maine. She touted $1.5 billion in federal funds that she has brought home to the state for 672 projects in the last five years, “from Madawaksa to Kittery, from Eastport to Rumford.” “I’ve been able to bring home federal dollars to help ease the burden on our taxpayers,” Collins said. Jackson set the tone for the debate early by connecting Collins to Trump and repeatedly saying she votes in alignment with him 96% of the time. Collins questioned the methodology of the study he cited. In a moment that captured her tricky relationship with her party’s leader , Collins dodged two questions about whether she would stand with Trump if he visited Maine, with Trump having recently teased a visit to the Pine Tree State. Collins said only that she doesn’t expect him to come and that she’s “not exactly his favorite senator.” Collins’ answer prompted a grin from Jackson. Trump has said Collins is “not my favorite person” but nevertheless endorsed her for re-election, and Vice President JD Vance has gone to Maine and backed her at events . Polls show a neck-and-neck race between Collins and Jackson, often within the margin of error, as Collins seeks to defy gravity yet again and win a sixth term in the blue-leaning state. She is the only GOP senator representing a state Trump lost in 2024. Both parties are spending tens of millions of dollars on a seat that carries major implications for control of the chamber, and a victory for Collins would constrict Democrats’ path to the Senate majority. Jackson also highlighted Collins’ pivotal vote in 2018 to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who was part of the majority that overturned Roe v. Wade, doing away with the federal right to abortion. Tuesday’s debate fell on the anniversary of Kavanaugh’s confirmation vote in the Senate. Collins said she judges all nominees by their qualifications, and she noted that she also supported justices who voted to uphold Roe v. Wade. “In fact, I am the only Republican senator to have voted for Justice [Sonia] Sotomayor, [Elena] Kagan and [Ketanji Brown] Jackson, who were nominated by a Democratic senator,” Collins said. Collins also hit back against attempts to tie her to the end of Roe v. Wade, referring to Jackson’s more conservative stance on abortion earlier in his career and quipping, “There’s only one of us on this stage who has always been pro-choice, and that’s me.” Jackson did not engage with the barb in the moment, but he noted in his closing statement that he pushed for progressive abortion policies in the Legislature. Jackson’s spokesperson, Dan Gottlieb, told NBC News earlier Tuesday that he would oppose any Trump Supreme Court nominee in his final two years should a vacancy open up — a view shared by some other Democrats . Jackson also said Collins voted to advance Trump’s “big, beautiful bill,” which included about $1 trillion in unpopular Medicaid cuts. That sparked a brushback from Collins, who noted that she voted against the legislation when it came to final passage. She said she has “never voted” to cut Medicaid. “He knows I voted against President Trump’s signature legislative accomplishment,” Collins said, adding that she used the process to support a $50 billion rural healthcare fund. Jackson doubled down. “Sen. Collins is like an arsonist who helped set the fire, and she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out,” he said. “She could have stopped it.” Collins went after Jackson’s “failed” policies as a state lawmaker, connecting them to higher housing costs and property taxes. She also questioned his talents as a legislator and whether he could be effective as a junior senator in a divided Senate. When the topic turned to immigration, Jackson cited an ICE officer’s killing of a Mainer this year, saying it happened because “Sen. Collins would not push back against ICE.” Collins said the shooting was “horrific” and “demonstrates that ICE needs further reform.” She said that she supported increased funding for body-worn cameras, as well as training of officers, and that she teamed up with the Maine delegation to demand answers from the Trump administration. In her closing statement, Collins said: “To be effective in the Senate, you need knowledge, experience, seniority and relationships. That combination has allowed me to pass bipartisan legislation.” Jackson questioned whether she has used her power well. “Tonight, Sen. Collins has told us how powerful she is,” he said in his closing statement. “But power means nothing if you won’t use it when the people may need it.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/susan-collins-troy-jackson-clash-trump-seniority-maines-first-senate-d-rcna601346

item.title: Washington resident accused of helping plan Canada's Tumbler Ridge school shooting
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
People pay their respects at a memorial on the steps of the Town Hall, following a vigil the previous day, in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, Canada, Feb. 14, 2026. - Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press/AP US authorities have arrested a 30-year-old from Washington state in connection with the February school shooting in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia. James Cody Bryant was arrested in Bellingham, Washington, on Tuesday morning on a charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country, according to the US Justice Department. The February attack on a secondary school in the small town at the foothills of the Rocky Mountains was Canada’s deadliest school shooting in decades, leaving eight people dead, including six children, and dozens wounded. Bryant appeared in court Tuesday afternoon in Seattle. CNN has reached out to Bryant’s lawyer for comment. A hearing has been set for October 20. Bryant was allegedly “in repeated contact with” the 18-year-old Canadian shooter, Jesse Van Rootselaar, “offering advice, sending money and even agreeing to live stream the horrific event” on Twitch, said Neil Floyd, the acting US attorney for the Western District of Washington, at a press conference in Seattle. The money Bryant gave the shooter amounted to a little over $100, primarily to buy a lighter and a pair of shoes that Van Rootselaar “wanted to have when she conducted this killing spree,” Floyd said. The two discussed sending weapons to Van Rootselaar, but Bryant was uncomfortable with doing so and refused, according to a complaint filed in court on Friday . Bryant began an online friendship with Van Rootselaar after meeting on video chatting website Omegle three years before the shooting, authorities said. An affidavit within the complaint includes excerpts of chat logs between Bryant and Van Rootselaar on the Discord website. “I read a lot of court documents, including some that discuss incredibly heinous acts of violence, but this complaint was particularly difficult to read,” said FBI agent Mike Harrington at the Tuesday press conference, “in part because of the casual tone these two individuals used when discussing the mass taking of innocent lives that was being planned.” In one exchange, Van Rootselaar allegedly told Bryant that she wanted to “avoid doing a school” but that “there’s just so many reasons why it’s ideal.” According to the affidavit, Bryant responded in turn that attacking a hotel “seems like a good idea.” After Van Rootselaar killed two family members, Bryant allegedly offered the attacker advice on how to fix a car when it failed to start en route to the school. Canadian and US authorities have said that Bryant and Van Rootselaar, who died in the shooting, are trans women, though officials used male and female pronouns interchangeably to describe the two throughout the press conference. Assistant Commissioner Elija Rain of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police said Canadian authorities contacted the US Department of Homeland Security soon after the shooting, based on “information from one of the online platforms used by the shooter.” “As further alleged, instead of de-escalating or reporting to law enforcement, Bryant continued to enable the shooter over the months they discussed these plans,” said Harrington. “In addition to providing money, technical advice and particular items to be used in the shooting, Bryant agreed to record a live stream feed of the attack and broadcast it in a way that would maximize notoriety for the shooter.” It was not previously known that anyone apart from Van Rootselaar allegedly participated in planning the massacre. CNN previously reported Van Rootselaar posted about guns and hunting and her apparent mental health struggles online in the lead up to the massacre. Seven families of victims sued tech company OpenAI in April after information emerged that the shooter had used ChatGPT to plan the attack. The week before the suit was filed, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman apologized to the community for not alerting law enforcement after Van Rootselaar’s account was banned. CNN’s Josh Campbell, Paula Newton and Lex Harvey contributed reporting. This story has been updated with additional developments. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/06/americas/arrest-tumbler-ridge-canada-shooting-latam-intl

item.title: Former CIA officer pleads guilty to stealing nearly $200 million in gold bar case
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The former CIA officer arrested after authorities discovered roughly $40 million worth of gold bars in his Virginia home pleaded guilty in federal court on Tuesday to a single count of wire fraud, admitting he defrauded the U.S. government out of nearly $200 million for his personal benefit. David Rush was previously described by prosecutors as a "master manipulator" who used his clandestine position to amass millions worth of gold bars and luxury watches -. though the government revealed in Tuesday's hearing the extent of his alleged deception far exceeded what was previously known to the public. The nearly $200 million in payments to Rush, which dwarfs previous amounts disclosed as part of his case, will likely only further draw public and congressional scrutiny to the intelligence community to provide more transparency regarding its methods in doling out taxpayer dollars to agents and the oversight that follows such exchanges. Alexandria's Sheriff's Office - PHOTO: In this image provided and annotated by the Alexandria's Sheriff's Office, David J. Rush is seen in his booking photo in Alexandria, Va. The case has drawn widespread intrigue and raised major questions regarding the intelligence community's management in overseeing the secretive systems that grant officials like Rush the ability to amass high-value assets tied to their work. Former CIA officer who had 303 gold bars in his home ordered detained According to a summary of his plea agreement provided by a senior DOJ prosecutor, Rush is alleged to have engaged in two separate criminal schemes where he fabricated so-called Special Access Programs to convince senior officials to clear payments to him totaling over $190 million that he sought to use for his personal benefit. In the first instance, prosecutors said Rush received approximately $145 million that he used to purchase luxury real estate properties in Palm Beach, Florida, and then carry out home improvements so he could then flip them and sell for a profit. Portions of the $145 million also went toward purchases of luxury vehicles and watches, all while Rush is alleged to have lied to officials that he had clearance for the payments from high-level officials in the Trump administration. A second scheme, prosecutors said, involved Rush's fabrication of a separate program that resulted in officials approving 298 gold bars to be provided to him that he later falsely claimed had been distributed, until the roughly $46.4 million worth of gold was discovered in a search of his residence in May. Rush also admitted to fraudulently seeking compensation for roughly $1.8 million in charter flights that were for his personal benefit. Another previously unreported disclosure from Tuesday's proceedings included an admission by Rush that he once disclosed top secret information to a foreign government official regarding the identity of a U.S. clandestine source. Prosecutors did not identify the foreign government who received the information or Rush's motives in sharing the source's identity, however. "Following an internal investigation that identified potential crimes, CIA immediately referred this matter to the FBI," said CIA Director John Ratcliffe. "David Rush abused his position and betrayed the public trust and should be held fully accountable for his actions. We appreciate our law enforcement partners in the FBI and Department of Justice for securing this outcome. The Agency is committed to ensuring that those entrusted with our Nation's secrets are held to the absolute highest standard." Attorney General Todd Blanche said, "Federal employees are entrusted with serving the American people, not themselves. The Trump Administration is committed to rooting out waste, fraud, and abuse in the federal government, including by prosecuting those who foolishly defraud American taxpayers." Rush has remained in government custody since his arrest in May, despite only facing initial charges of theft of public money that accused him lying about his background and committing time card fraud regarding claims about military leave. The single wire fraud charge Rush pleaded guilty to Tuesday carries a maximum potential sentence of 20 years in prison and Rush separately agreed to $195 million in restitution as part of his plea. Rush's sentencing has been set for Jan. 28 of next year. This article originally appeared on Good Morning America at https://abcnews.com/Politics/plea-hearing-set-former-cia-officer-allegedly-gold/story?id=137015337

item.title: Army sets date for Fort Hood mass shooter Nidal Hasan to face firing squad
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Nidal Hasan, who was sentenced to death for the 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, will be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3, according to a memo from the acting Army secretary. The execution, the first carried out by the U.S. military in more than 60 years, is scheduled for 1 p.m. CT, according to the memo issued Tuesday by acting Army Secretary Adam Telle. The Pentagon announced Monday that Hasan would be executed by firing squad after President Donald Trump approved the decision Friday. Handout/Getty Images - PHOTO: Maj. Nidal Hasan Moved To Jail Under the military’s execution process for prisoners on death row, the Army secretary initiates the proceedings, which then require approval from the defense secretary and eventually the president. Under Army policy, executions must happen within 150 days of the president approving it, but no sooner than 60 days. The military has not executed a service member since 1961, when Pvt. John Bennett was put to death after being convicted of the rape and attempted murder of an 11-year-old girl in Austria. On Nov. 5, 2009, Hasan, then an Army psychiatrist, opened fire at the Soldier Readiness Processing Center at the Fort Hood military base, killing 12 soldiers and one civilian before he was shot, severely wounded and arrested. Hasan was convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted murder and sentenced to death in 2013. He was sent to a military detention center at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas. He is one of four death row inmates in the Army justice system. The announcement of his execution comes after ABC News reported in June that the Army had been planning military executions , according to internal documents and officials familiar with the matter. Army regulation dictates that at least two media outlets should be selected to witness the execution. item.title: Most families of troops killed in the Iran war's deadliest attack weren't at White House event
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Relatives of some soldiers killed in the Iran war joined dozens of Gold Star families from prior U.S. conflicts Tuesday at the White House, where President Donald Trump offered words of comfort and candles were lit for the fallen service members, according to one of the widows who attended. Not all families of the six soldiers killed March 1 in the deadliest attack of the Iran war opted to attend. Troops who survived the attack have raised questions about why they were stationed at a site that didn’t have sufficient air protection and was viewed as a likely target. Michelle Tietjens and other relatives have said they are angry the Army still hasn’t answered questions over whether enough was done to protect their loved ones. But Tietjens and her teenage son traveled from Bellevue, Nebraska, to attend the event to honor her husband, Master Sgt. Noah Tietjens, who was killed along with five other Army Reserve soldiers by an Iranian drone strike in Kuwait. “I decided to go originally because my son wanted to go,” Tietjens said. “But then I wanted to see what it was about as well. I wanted to also go to support my husband's memory.” She said they toured several rooms of the White House and took a photo with Trump and the first lady, Melania Trump. Tietjens said the president told them that he wished he had her teenage son's full head of curly hair. Tietjens said the reception “didn’t change my feelings on them giving me answers,” and added that she spoke with someone at the White House who offered to try to help. The annual gathering honors Gold Star Mother’s and Family’s Day, which falls on the last weekend of September. The White House said this year’s reception honored nearly 40 fallen service members from conflicts dating to the Vietnam War. The Iran war, launched Feb. 28, has claimed the lives of 19 U.S. troops and wounded more than 800 others. Tietjens said she also saw at the reception family members of Maj. Jeffrey R. O’Brien, who was also killed at Port Shuaiba, and of Pfc. Isabella Gonzalez, who was killed July 17 in an Iranian attack at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan. Families are still waiting for answers about what happened in the March 1 strike Gold Star families have expressed frustration over the lack of information from the Pentagon about the strike in Kuwait. “There are questions about what happened before the attack, what information was available, what decisions were made, and what happened in the moments leading up to six American soldiers losing their lives,” Joey Amor — whose 39-year-old wife, Master Sgt. Nicole M. Amor, was among those killed — said in a public Facebook statement Monday. “I am done asking quietly. Today, I am asking the American people to stand with these six families and demand transparency.” U.S. soldiers wounded in the attack told The Associated Press of the unheeded concerns they raised about the threat and said the military medical system failed them in the weeks that followed. The AP’s account of the March 1 attack is based on interviews with 13 soldiers. The Army declined to comment on the AP’s reporting on the Port Shuaiba strike, saying it had not yet briefed the families of those killed on the outcome of its investigation into the attack, which was completed in June. The Army has said it is still redacting sensitive information before releasing the findings. The Pentagon also declined to comment. Honoring soldiers who died in combat can be a powerful recognition of their service that cuts across politics, said John Thompson, a former Army sergeant and founder of Salute to the Fallen, an Iowa organization that supports veteran mental health, suicide prevention and funeral expenses. He said several families told him they could not go because they did not receive enough notice about the event. At least two families say they did not receive an invitation The White House began sending out invitations to Gold Star families — the military’s designation for relatives of troops killed while on active duty — about two weeks ago, according to several families who said they received phone calls and emailed invitations. “What they’ve told me is there has been a lot of confusion around this event, and they weren’t given the details in time,” Thompson said, adding that some were also not in a position to pay for the trip. At least two said they did not receive an invite, though there can be hurdles to tracking down families' personal information. Some Gold Star families say they are grateful for how the Trump administration and military have honored their loved one’s sacrifice. Other families say the way the White House has handled the reception is the latest indication that the administration does not respect the price they have paid. In the early days of the war, Trump described it as a “little excursion ." On Sept. 4, he called the conflict “small potatoes.” The widow of Chief Warrant Officer 3 Robert Marzan, who died in the March 1 attack, said she and her two children were not invited. Tina Marzan said that in the immediate aftermath of her husband’s death, she told federal officials she did not want to be contacted after receiving multiple calls. But she had hoped they would have tried to reach her or others in her family for an event like this, she said. “We should be there,” Tina Marzan told the AP. “I mean, that’s not a question.” The White House said it honors people's requests not to be contacted. Donna Burhans, the mother of Maj. Cody Khork, who was one of those killed at Port Shuaiba, said she did not receive an invitation but would not have attended because it's too painful. She has described herself as a “big fan” of Trump after meeting him during the dignified transfer at Dover Air Force Base. “I just can’t keep going thru (sic) this over and over,” she told the AP in a text message. The White House said it attempted to send invitations to Khork's family members. The spouse of Maj. Alex Klinner , an airman who was killed in an Iran-related combat operation this summer, said receiving less than two weeks’ notice did not give her enough time to arrange for overnight care for her three young children. In a text message, Libby Klinner said she would not have gone anyway, adding, “I have no interest in supporting an administration that has been so reckless with the lives of our service members." ___ Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia, and Brook reported from New Orleans. Associated Press writers Julie Watson in San Diego, Allen G. Breed in Wake Forest, North Carolina, and Collin Binkley in Washington contributed to this report. item.title: Fake Jane Does are flooding the internet to protect the plaintiff in Cornell rape case
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Supporters have launched an online campaign in recent weeks aimed at protecting the identity of a woman, identified as " Jane Doe , " who alleges in a civil lawsuit that she was drugged and raped by multiple members of a Cornell University fraternity in 2024. Jane Doe's lawyer says that the ex-Cornell student has received " multiple threats " in recent days aimed at exposing her real identity. "There are people out there trying to track her down," Thomas Giuffra, who ‌represents Jane Doe, told CNN's State of the Union on Sunday. "They said, 'We're gonna shut you up. You're gonna still get hurt by us. You're gonna pull this lawsuit out or we're gonna do something to hurt you even more.' "The threats, the abuse to protect what's going on, the status quo — these guys are disgusting," Giuffra added. Among those trying to identify Jane Doe is political commentator Michael Tracey, who publicly asked anyone with information about her identity to contact him and said he would publish her name and identifying details. The possibility that Jane Doe's true identity might be revealed mobilized many social media users to post "I am Jane Doe" in an effort to protect the identity of the former Cornell University student. Hundreds of Cornell students participated in a rally about the rape case on Oct. 5 in Ithaca. Spencer Platt/Getty Images The goal of the movement is to show solidarity with Jane Doe and to make online searches for the woman's identity less useful by returning a mix of conflicting "Jane Doe" identities. Some TikTok users have been sharing their own experiences with sexual assault and overlaying "I am Jane Doe" text over the video. In a Reddit thread , some users are taking it a step further by deliberately using false identities, including fictional characters or celebrities. "Jane Doe's name? Nunya. Nunya Business," one user commented. "Of course I know the identity of Jane Doe, the plaintiff against Cornell and the Cornell 7. Jane Doe is Robert California," another user wrote, referring to the fictional character from The Office . According to Chirag Shah, a professor at the University of Washington's Information School, the tactic has a name. "Typically, this is a form of information poisoning," Shah told Yahoo. "People do it for different intents to confuse people, to slow them down or to divert them to other things." Shah said this strategy is commonly associated with misinformation campaigns, online scams and efforts to manipulate search results. He said this recent strategy stands out because many participants appear to be motivated to protect the plaintiff's identity. "If the intent here is to protect Jane Doe, which, on the social side of it, is very admirable, on the technical side of it, it's not really possible," Shah said. "But what it ends up doing is creating friction." He explained that while the friction might discourage casual internet sleuths, it's unlikely to conceal someone's identity from those determined to uncover it. "Most people don't have the time, motivation or skills to really investigate," Shah said. "But somebody who really wants to do this, they can cut through this noise." An attendee wears a name tag reading "Jane Doe" during an Oct. 5 protest in Ithaca. Adrian Kraus/AP The online movement has sparked discussion about whether flooding the internet with false identities could confuse search engines and AI chatbots. Shah said modern systems are designed to combat attempts by bad actors to spread false information. "Because this is not a new phenomenon, the existing search engines, including the chatbots, are designed to counteract a lot of these things," Shah said. "Even if it works, it would only work temporarily." Search engines also increasingly weigh the credibility and reliability of sources rather than simply counting mentions of a claim, he explained. A surge of coordinated posts might temporarily influence results, but Shah said those systems are built to recognize unusual spikes and eventually correct for them. Volume can still matter in specific ways, he added. If "I am Jane Doe" posts are associated with one celebrity's name, it will generate more volume and receive more attention, but it could easily be discredited if the celebrity clearly is not the former Cornell student. "If the intent is to leave people confused, you're better off giving all kinds of [names]," Shah said, comparing it to the "Two Truths and a Lie" game. "If you tell a million lies and one is true, it's much harder to find, and people then just give up. "So that strategy often works." Shah said the campaign itself is fascinating to him because it flips a tactic usually used by bad actors into one being used by people who believe they are protecting someone vulnerable. "All these times I have talked about misinformation and disinformation campaigns, this is the first time it's sort of on this side," Shah said. "If I were ever to look for a good case of a misinformation campaign," he added, "this would be it." item.title: FBI whistleblower says White House pushed unconstitutional probe of protesters
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON — The Trump administration pushed the FBI to investigate Los Angeles protesters in violation of their constitutional rights and the bureau’s policies, a former FBI supervisor alleges in a new whistleblower complaint. Jill Fields, a former supervisory intelligence analyst in the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, made a formal whistleblower complaint to Senate Judiciary Committee leaders over the federal response to anti-ICE protest activity around federal buildings, as well as in a residential area, early last year. Fields asked Congress and the Justice Department’s watchdog to investigate the allegations, her attorneys said in a letter to lawmakers. She says they violated the First Amendment right to free speech and to peaceably assemble. Fields says Emil Bove, then the acting deputy attorney general, told the head of the field office to open an investigation into activities outside the federal building even though, she says, the activities were protected free speech. Separately, she says the White House gave a directive to FBI Director Kash Patel to investigate a group of protesters using megaphones during immigration enforcement operations after FBI agents had conducted a check into the conduct and declined to open an investigation. President Donald Trump had viewed a video of people using megaphones to alert residents about immigration activities, advise them of their legal rights and encourage them not to open their doors unless immigration enforcement agents had signed judicial warrants, according to the letter. A person whose name is redacted in the complaint told Fields that an investigation would be opened because “the President wants this investigation,” Fields’ whistleblower complaint says. The protests were staged across Los Angeles after the Trump administration launched an immigration enforcement operation. Fields said the FBI’s Los Angeles office had pulled agents off active cartel cases to satisfy what a supervisor described as “optics” designed to “make a show for the president.” The area would be the scene of major protests later in the year during an immigration surge in cities nationwide. A Justice Department spokesperson called the whistleblower complaint politically motivated and said violence is not protected by the First Amendment, though the complaint focused on nonviolent protests. “Under President Trump, the Department of Justice will continue to vigorously uphold the First Amendment rights of all Americans and restore the rule of law,” the spokesperson said. “The DOJ and FBI have a responsibility to investigate any potential violations of federal law, and conspiracies to impede federal law enforcement and assaults on federal officers are against the law.” The FBI didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Justice Department officials have previously said government workers need to follow the Trump administration’s priorities. Last week, Justice Department leaders filed an administrative complaint about federal judges who made remarks to the media about the impact the surge in immigration enforcement had on their courtrooms. Fields says supervisors were told not to put things in writing, so many of the directives came in face-to-face meetings. She says she didn’t know whether any formal investigation was opened because she was excluded once she refused to participate. Fields consulted with a senior FBI official in charge of privacy and civil liberties matters, who expressed dismay about the investigation and subsequently told Fields she planned to resign, according to the complaint. Fields, too, resigned from the bureau, after she was informed that she would be removed from heading three programs, a decision she believes constituted retaliation for making protected internal disclosures. The FBI’s actions, according to the letter, “created a chilling effect within the workforce” and “signaled to other employees that raising constitutional or legal concerns could carry professional consequences.” The conduct “had significant consequences for constitutional rights, and the integrity and effective operation of the FBI,” according to the complaint. Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif. (Tom Williams / CQ Roll Call via Getty) Hundreds of FBI agents and Justice Department attorneys have resigned or been fired since Trump returned to office , particularly those who were involved in investigating him, and former Justice Department employees have expressed concerns that the nation’s top law enforcement agency is doing the bidding of the president. Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., told NBC News that Fields’ disclosure is another instance of Trump’s weaponizing the Justice Department to go after his perceived political enemies. Padilla, who himself was forcibly removed from a news conference featuring then-Homeland Security Kristi Noem in June 2025 , is the ranking member of the Judiciary subcommittee on immigration, citizenship and border safety. “How many more of these investigations have been opened up because of political pressure coming from the White House, despite the questions and concerns about legality and constitutionality?” Padilla said. He acknowledged that the Trump administration’s attacks on civil service protections through unilateral firings, as well as the mass firings of internal government watchdogs , had an impact on the legislative branch’s ability to conduct oversight. “That’s going to be a significant challenge, but it begins with good, honorable professionals being willing to come forward and tell us what’s going on and what’s wrong with what’s going on,” Padilla said. “We’re hoping others may be inspired, as well.” In a letter he sent to Patel and Attorney General Todd Blanche, Padilla wrote that the allegations in the Fields disclosure “raise grave concerns about the rule of law under your leadership, the diversion of resources from ongoing criminal investigations, and the testimony that you provided under oath to Congress.” He asked for officials to preserve information about the investigation and send any details to his office. Fields was represented by the nonprofit Government Accountability Project and David Laufman, a former top official in the Justice Department’s National Security Section.
